title: Universal vertices and effective dimension in geometric-graph entropy
shortTitle: Some points in a random geometric graph cost no bits
oneLine: Storing a random geometric graph with n vertices takes d(1 − μ(Uᵣ)) n log₂ n bits up to O(n), where Uᵣ is the set of positions joined to everyone; this refutes the exact cube coefficient conjectured by Vippathalla, Coon and Badiu for d ≥ 2 and √d/2 < r < √d, and proves their torus conjecture at every radius.
abstract: How many bits does it take to store a random geometric graph? Scatter n labelled points in a d-dimensional region with a density bounded above and away from zero, join two of them when they are within a fixed distance r, and ask for the Shannon entropy H(Gₙ) of the resulting graph. A heuristic says d n log₂ n: each of the d coordinates of each point is pinned down to about 1/n by the others. This candidate shows exactly when that is right and what replaces it. On every compact convex domain and for every fixed radius, H(Gₙ) = d(1 − μ(Uᵣ)) n log₂ n + O(n), where Uᵣ is the set of universal positions, within distance r of the whole domain: a vertex there is joined to everyone, so its position carries no information. For translation rules of finite perimeter on the flat torus, which may have holes or several pieces, the coefficient is the rank of the lattice generated by the rule's nonzero Fourier frequencies, the number of independent directions the rule can detect. For the unit cube this refutes the exact-coefficient reading of the conjecture of Vippathalla, Coon and Badiu (ISIT 2026; as stated in arXiv:2601.10778v1) at every radius between √d/2 and √d when d ≥ 2: in the unit square at r = 1 the coefficient is 2√3 − 2π/3 ≈ 1.3697, not ≈ 1.4610, and the gap peaks at about 0.161 near r ≈ 1.13. The conjecture's order of growth holds in every case, and its exact coefficients hold for smaller radii, in dimension one and on the torus at every 0 < r < √d/2, each with an O(n) remainder. The radius dependence of every error term is explicit. All results concern a fixed radius as n grows. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Convex domains: for every compact convex body D ⊂ ℝᵈ, density bounded above and below, and fixed r > 0, H(Gₙ) = d(1 − μ(Uᵣ)) n log₂ n + O(n), where Uᵣ = {x ∈ D : D ⊆ B̄(x, r)} is the set of universal positions (Theorem 3.1, proof).

Cube correction: for d ≥ 2 and √d/2 < r < √d the earlier conjectured coefficient d[1 − β(r)] is strictly larger than the true d[1 − u_d(r)], so the exact-coefficient reading of the conjecture in arXiv:2601.10778v1 is false there; its upper bounds remain valid (Proposition 4.1, proof).

Unit square, r = 1: coefficient 2√3 − 2π/3 ≈ 1.3697 instead of ≈ 1.4610, 6.25% lower; across the square the gap peaks at about 0.161 near r ≈ 1.13 (18.7% of the earlier coefficient), and the relative gap at about 20.9% near r ≈ 1.17 (Corollary 4.2, proof; exact SymPy identity; gap curve numerical).

Fourier rank: for an even finite-perimeter translation rule b on the torus, the coefficient is the rank of the lattice generated by the nonzero Fourier frequencies of b, the number of directions the rule can detect (Theorem 5.1, proof).
Torus: the coefficient is d for every 0 < r < √d/2, proving the torus conjecture of arXiv:2601.10778v1 beyond the previously proved r ≤ 1/4 (Corollary 5.6, proof).
Confirmed elsewhere: the n log n order in every case, the cube coefficient d for r ≤ √d/2, and dimension one at every radius, each with an O(n) remainder (Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.5).

Radius dependence: the upper remainders are uniform in r; the proved lower remainders grow like log(1/r) as r → 0 and, on the torus, like d² log₂(1/(√d/2 − r)) per vertex near the endpoint (Propositions 3.4 and 5.7, proof).

narration: Some points in a random geometric graph cost no bits. An Evidence Press briefing. First, the background: scatter points at random in a region, and join any two that lie within a fixed distance of each other. Networks like this model wireless sensors, contacts and spatial infrastructure. A natural question is how many bits it takes, on average, to store such a network with n points. The rough answer is d times n times the logarithm of n, because each point has d coordinates, and the rest of the network pins each one down to about one part in n. Next, the question: in 2026, Vippathalla, Coon and Badiu proved upper bounds for the cube and the torus, and conjectured that their leading terms were exactly right. Now, the main finding: on any convex region, and for every fixed distance, the leading cost is d times the fraction of points that are not universal, times n log n. A universal point is within reach of every possible position, so it is joined to everyone, and its links reveal nothing about where it is. Such points cost nothing. In the unit square at distance one, about thirty-one and a half per cent of points are universal, and the true coefficient is about 1.370, not the conjectured 1.461. So the exact cube conjecture is false at every radius between half the diagonal and the full diagonal, in two or more dimensions. It is confirmed elsewhere: for smaller radii, in one dimension, and on the torus at every radius, where every direction is visible. For more general connection rules on the torus, the coefficient counts the directions the rule can detect. As for how sure this is: every theorem has a written proof, and the computations are sanity checks. Finally, the limits: the results are for a fixed distance as n grows, and they do not identify the next term. It is an anonymous, unrefereed candidate, with AI-assisted review only, not peer review. Published on 27 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: A written proof refutes the exact-coefficient reading of the 2026 Vippathalla–Coon–Badiu cube conjecture for d ≥ 2 and √d/2 < r < √d (unit square at r = 1: 2√3 − 2π/3 instead of about 1.461), determines the entropy coefficient on every convex domain and for finite-perimeter torus rules, and proves their torus conjecture at every radius.
decisionObject.scope: Labelled hard geometric graphs with fixed dimension and fixed radius, independent positions with a density bounded above and away from zero, n → ∞; conjecture statements as in arXiv:2601.10778v1. The coefficient of n, shrinking radii, structural entropy for d ≥ 2 and efficient encoders are not addressed.
